messages.author: 4719990e9dfe6605
messages.subject: eQTL FDR through permutations
parts:
I’m conducting an eQTL study in a RIL mapping population. One
challenge is figuring out how to control for multiple testing with
thousands of transcripts. One method I've seen in the literature is
an empirically derived FDR using permutations (Brem et al. 2002 in
Science, Smith & Kruglyak 2008 in PLoS Bio, Rockman et al. 2010 in
Science). I would like to use this approach as a way to determine an
FDR threshold for my R/qtl scanone results.

The approach focuses on permuting the row labels of all of the
transcripts. This will maintain the correlation structure among
expression traits while randomizing the individual genotype vectors
associated with each phenotype vector. After each round of
permutation, I will extract the single highest LOD score per each
phenotype. This will result in a vector with ~25000 LOD scores, one
LOD score for each transcript. I plan to conduct many such rounds of
permutations and then use the results to calculate an FDR. To do so I
will rank the LOD scores per each round and then calculate the mean
LOD per rank across all permutation rounds. To calculate FDR = 0.05,
I will determine the LOD at which only 5% of the mean LOD scores are
ranked larger. This FDR threshold will then be applied to the output
of interval mapping in the nonpermuted data as a threshold for QTL
significance across the entire data set. Does this method seem
reasonable?

I’ve written some scripts to run this type of analysis but it is
computational intensive and involves several manipulations of data
outputs. I’m wondering whether much of the existing scanone and
summary.scanoneperm will let me do a similar analysis. For example,
if I run permutations on all my phenotypes together (phe.col= 1:25000)
are these completed by shuffling row labels (maintaining the
correlations structure)? Also, the summary documentation mentions an
argument “controlAcrossCol” of “summary.scanoneperm.” In that
documentation you write:

“If ‘controlAcrossCol=TRUE’, we use a trick to control the error rate
not just across the genome but also across the LOD score columns.
Namely, we convert each column of permutation results to ranks, and
then for each permutation replicate we find the maximum rank across
the columns. We then find the appropriate quantile of the maximized
ranks, and then backtrack to the corresponding LOD score within each
of the columns.”

Is this implementing the “FDR” approach I describe above? Please let
me know if I am misinterpreting this and thanks for your help.

David

messages.author: 96353e7106735838
messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] eQTL FDR through permutations
parts: On Jan 11, 2012, at 10:30 AM, David Lowry <davidbry...@gmail.com> wrote:

> For example,
> if I run permutations on all my phenotypes together (phe.col= 1:25000)
> are these completed by shuffling row labels (maintaining the
> correlations structure)?
Yes, the correlation among phenotypes is preserved. We permute the rows in the phenotype data relative to the rows in the genotype data.

> Also, the summary documentation mentions an
> argument “controlAcrossCol” of “summary.scanoneperm.” In that
> documentation you write:
>
> “If ‘controlAcrossCol=TRUE’, we use a trick to control the error rate
> not just across the genome but also across the LOD score columns.
> Namely, we convert each column of permutation results to ranks, and
> then for each permutation replicate we find the maximum rank across
> the columns. We then find the appropriate quantile of the maximized
> ranks, and then backtrack to the corresponding LOD score within each
> of the columns.”
>
> Is this implementing the “FDR” approach I describe above? Please let
> me know if I am misinterpreting this and thanks for your help.

This doesn't use FDR but rather seeks to control the family-wise error rate (FWER).

karl

messages.author: 04e62c3b36bb17bf
messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] eQTL FDR through permutations
parts:
Hi Karl et al. 
I am trying to control GWER for a single scan and FDR across multiple phenotypes for one-way QTL scans. 

In my experiment, we have 16k expression phenotypes. When I summarize the 1000 scanone permutations using controlAcrossCol = T, it always returns the maximum permutation value for each phenotype, even when alpha is set at 0.5 or higher. I also ran 10k permutations and ran into the same issue. I think this is just a product of making thousands of tests, not an issue with the function. 

Do you have any advice about the best way forward? I don't think using the maximum observed permutation is a particularly good threshold. Doing more permutations (>100k), might solve the problem, but would be a pretty big computational load. What about modelling the distribution of permutations and finding the (alpha/npheno) quantile of the predicted distribution? 

Any advice is much appreciated,
John

messages.author: 96353e7106735838
messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] eQTL FDR through permutations
parts:
Using controlAcrossCol=TRUE (or alpha/n_pheno) would both be seeking to control the overall family-wise error rate: if none of the expression phenotypes are affected by a QTL, have just 5% chance of any of them showing significant results. You'll need a *lot* more permutations, maybe on the order of **16 million**, because you have to go way out into the tail of the marginal distributions.

The results you're getting suggest that >50% of the time, at least one of the 16k phenotypes has a LOD score that is above the 99.9% quantile of its marginal null distribution.

You could try doing FDR across the expression traits, as you'd mentioned in your first paragraph: get the p-value of the biggest LOD score for each of the 16k traits, and then turn those into q-values, for example with the bioconductor package qvalue.

karl

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] eQTL FDR through permutations
parts:
Thanks Karl - this makes total sense. 
I'll do some thinking about how best to do FDR ... maybe pull the max LOD for each chromosome for each trait, calculate permutation p-values and transform via qvalue. The only issue here is that the p-values will have a bounded left tail (given a finite number of permutations), which might violate some of the assumptions of qvalue. 
Cheers, John
